Topic 1: What is Data?

Definition

Data is a collection of raw facts and figures that by themselves may not have any meaning.

Think of data as unprocessed information.

Example:

Shashank
21
Delhi
9876543210

These are just facts.

Another example:

95
88
76
100
91

These are just numbers.

Until we know whose marks these are, they don't provide useful information.

Data vs Information

This is one of the favourite interview questions.

Data

Raw facts.

Example

Roll No: 231B214
Marks: 95

Information

Processed data that has meaning.

Example

Shashank scored 95 marks in DBMS and secured Rank 2.

Now it tells a story.

Real Life Example

Imagine Flipkart.

Raw Data:

Order ID: 2312
Amount: ₹2500
Customer: Rahul
Date: 15 July

Information:

Rahul spent ₹2500 on electronics on 15 July.

Now the company can analyse customer behaviour.

Types of Data

1. Structured Data

Stored in rows and columns.

Example

IDNameAge
1Rahul20
2Amit22

SQL databases store structured data.

Examples

  • MySQL

  • PostgreSQL

  • Oracle

2. Semi-Structured Data

Has some structure but not fixed tables.

Example JSON

JSON
{
   "name":"Shashank",
   "age":21,
   "skills":["React","Node","MongoDB"]
}

Examples

  • JSON

  • XML

3. Unstructured Data

No predefined structure.

Examples

  • Images

  • Videos

  • Audio

  • PDF

  • Emails

Instagram photos are unstructured data.

Characteristics of Good Data

  • Accurate

  • Complete

  • Consistent

  • Timely

  • Relevant

Interview Question

What is the difference between Data and Information?

Answer:

Data is raw facts without context, whereas information is processed data that has meaning and can help in decision-making.

Topic 2: What is a Database?

Imagine your phone.

It stores

  • Contacts

  • Photos

  • Notes

  • WhatsApp chats

All this data is organised somewhere.

That organised collection is called a database.

Definition

A database is an organised collection of related data that can be easily accessed, managed, and updated.

Example

Student Table

Roll NoNameBranchCGPA
231B214ShashankCSE8.81
231B115GatikCSE8.75

This table is part of a database.

Real World Examples

Instagram

Database stores

  • Username

  • Followers

  • Following

  • Posts

  • Likes

  • Comments

Swiggy

Database stores

  • Restaurants

  • Menu

  • Orders

  • Delivery Partner

  • Payments

Banking

Database stores

  • Account Number

  • Balance

  • Transactions

  • Loans

Database Characteristics

A good database should

  • Store huge amounts of data

  • Allow quick searching

  • Allow updates

  • Avoid duplication

  • Keep data secure

  • Support multiple users

Topic 3: What is DBMS?

Now suppose the database exists.

How will users interact with it?

There must be software between users and the database.

That software is called DBMS.

Definition

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that allows users to create, manage, update, retrieve, and control databases.

Simply put:

Database = Storage

DBMS = Manager of that storage

Diagram

        User

          │

          ▼

      DBMS Software

          │

          ▼

      Database Files

The user never directly edits the database files. They send requests to the DBMS, which safely handles the data.

Example

Suppose you search

Amazon → "iPhone 16"

Amazon's backend sends a query to the DBMS.

The DBMS searches millions of records.

It returns matching products.

Popular DBMS

  • MySQL

  • PostgreSQL

  • Oracle

  • SQL Server

  • SQLite

What can a DBMS do?

  • Create databases

  • Create tables

  • Insert data

  • Update data

  • Delete data

  • Search data

  • Provide security

  • Handle backups

  • Manage multiple users

Interview Question

Difference between Database and DBMS?

Database = collection of data.

DBMS = software that manages that collection.

Topic 4: Why Do We Need DBMS?

Imagine the early days of computing.

People didn't have databases.

Everything was stored in files.

student.txt
employee.txt
marks.txt
fees.txt

This is called the File System.

Problems with File Systems

1. Data Redundancy

The same data is stored multiple times.

Example

Student.txt

Rahul
Age 20
Delhi

Fees.txt

Rahul
Age 20
Delhi

The same information appears in multiple files.

This wastes storage and increases maintenance effort.

2. Data Inconsistency

Suppose Rahul changes his address.

You update Student.txt.

But forget to update Fees.txt.

Now the same student has two different addresses in different files.

Which one is correct?

This inconsistency leads to unreliable data.

3. Difficult Searching

Finding records in plain text files is slow.

If a company has

50 lakh records

Searching manually through files is inefficient.

4. No Security

Anyone with access to the file can read or modify it.

There is no fine-grained control.

5. No Backup

If the file is accidentally deleted, all data may be lost.

6. No Concurrent Access

If two employees edit the same file simultaneously, one person's changes might overwrite the other's.

7. Data Isolation

Information is scattered across many separate files, making it difficult to combine or analyse.

Solution: DBMS

A DBMS solves these problems by providing

  • Centralised storage

  • Data consistency

  • Security

  • Backup and recovery

  • Multi-user access

  • Fast searching

  • Reduced redundancy

File System vs DBMS

FeatureFile SystemDBMS
RedundancyHighLow
SecurityPoorStrong
BackupManualBuilt-in support
SearchingSlowFast
Multi-user supportLimitedExcellent
ConsistencyPoorGood
Data relationshipsDifficultEasy with keys and relations

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a library.

Without a DBMS (File System)

Every book is piled randomly on the floor.

Finding a book takes a long time.

Multiple copies of the same book may exist.

Books can be lost easily.

With a DBMS

Books are organised by category, author, and shelf.

You can search quickly.

Only authorised staff can update records.

Everything is tracked.

Topic 5: Advantages & Disadvantages of DBMS

Advantages

1. Reduced Data Redundancy

Duplicate data is minimised by designing related tables properly.

2. Better Consistency

When data changes, it is updated in a controlled way, reducing conflicting values.

3. Security

Access can be controlled using user accounts and permissions.

Example:

  • Admin: Full access

  • Employee: Read and update

  • Customer: Limited access

4. Backup & Recovery

Most DBMSs provide tools to recover data after failures.

5. Data Sharing

Many users can access the database at the same time.

6. Data Integrity

Rules (called constraints) ensure only valid data is stored.

For example, an age field cannot contain the text "Hello" if it expects numbers.

7. Fast Retrieval

Indexes and query optimisation help fetch data quickly even from very large databases.

8. Centralised Control

All data is managed from one central system, making administration easier.

Disadvantages

1. High Cost

Enterprise DBMS software and infrastructure can be expensive.

2. Complexity

Designing and maintaining databases requires skilled professionals.

3. Large Size

DBMS software itself can consume significant storage and memory.

4. Performance Overhead

For very small applications, a simple file may sometimes be faster than using a full DBMS because of additional management layers.

5. Failure Impact

If the central database server fails and there is no proper backup or failover, many users may be affected.

Placement Interview Questions (Must Know)

  1. What is data? How is it different from information?

  2. What is a database?

  3. What is DBMS?

  4. What is the difference between a database and a DBMS?

  5. Why was DBMS introduced instead of file systems?

  6. Explain the problems with the file system approach.

  7. What is data redundancy? Give a real-life example.

  8. What is data inconsistency? How does DBMS solve it?

  9. List the advantages of a DBMS.

  10. What are the disadvantages of a DBMS?

These five topics form the conceptual foundation of DBMS. Once you're comfortable with them, the next step is the Relational Model, where you'll learn about tables, rows, columns, attributes, tuples, schemas, instances, and domains—the building blocks of every SQL database.

Interview Questions

Q1 Why is MySQL called a Relational Database?

Because it stores data in related tables connected using keys such as primary keys and foreign keys.

Q2 Why does Instagram use NoSQL?

Because Instagram handles billions of posts, comments, messages, and media. NoSQL databases offer flexible schemas and can scale horizontally across many servers to manage such large and rapidly changing workloads.

Q3 Which database is best?

There is no universal "best" database. The right choice depends on the application's needs:

  • Banking → Relational (strong consistency)

  • Social Media → NoSQL (scalability and flexibility)

  • Analytics → Column databases

  • Recommendation engines → Graph databases

Topic 7: Database Users

Not everyone interacts with a database in the same way. Different people have different responsibilities.

Database Users
│
├── Database Administrator (DBA)
├── Database Designers
├── Application Programmers
├── End Users
└── Database Analysts

Let's understand each.

1. Database Administrator (DBA) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

The DBA is the person responsible for managing and maintaining the database.

Responsibilities:

  • Install DBMS software

  • Create databases

  • Manage users

  • Grant permissions

  • Backup and recovery

  • Monitor performance

  • Ensure security

  • Tune queries and indexes

Think of a DBA as the "manager" of the database.

2. Database Designer

Designs the database before development begins.

Responsibilities:

  • Decide which tables are needed

  • Define relationships

  • Choose primary and foreign keys

  • Apply normalization

  • Create the schema

Example:
Before building a college management system, the designer plans tables such as Student, Course, Faculty, and Enrollment.

3. Application Programmer (Developer)

Writes the application that communicates with the database.

Responsibilities:

  • Write SQL queries

  • Build APIs

  • Insert and retrieve data

  • Connect frontend and backend with the database

Example:
A Node.js backend developer writing SQL queries to fetch products from PostgreSQL.

4. End Users

The people who actually use the application.

Examples:

  • Students using a college portal

  • Customers shopping on Amazon

  • Users posting on Instagram

End users usually don't write SQL directly; they interact through the application's interface.

5. Database Analyst

Studies data and business requirements.

Responsibilities:

  • Understand business needs

  • Recommend database improvements

  • Generate reports

  • Analyse trends and performance

Topic 8: Database Administrator (DBA) in Detail

Although we've introduced the DBA above, interviewers often ask specifically about this role.

Who is a DBA?

A Database Administrator is responsible for the installation, maintenance, security, performance, and availability of the database.

Key Responsibilities

1. Installation and Configuration

  • Install the DBMS

  • Configure storage and memory settings

2. User Management

  • Create users

  • Reset passwords

  • Assign roles and permissions

3. Security

  • Prevent unauthorised access

  • Manage authentication and authorisation

4. Backup and Recovery

  • Schedule backups

  • Restore data after failures

5. Performance Tuning

  • Monitor slow queries

  • Create indexes

  • Optimise database performance

6. Monitoring

  • Track CPU, memory, storage, and query performance

  • Detect bottlenecks

7. High Availability

  • Configure replication and failover

  • Minimise downtime

Skills Required for a DBA

  • Strong SQL knowledge

  • Backup and recovery techniques

  • Indexing

  • Query optimisation

  • Security concepts

  • Operating system basics

  • Networking fundamentals
